purpose: Show where each workstation tool fits in one change: from a new branch to a merged pull request.
explanation: GitHub flow (GitHub Docs) is: create a branch, make and commit changes, push, open a pull request, address review comments, merge, then delete the branch. The editor step uses the VS Code debugger (VS Code docs, Debugging). The commit message follows the Conventional Commits 1.0.0 format, so tools can build release notes from history. Review can send the change back to the editor before it is merged.
alt: Flowchart: create a branch, edit and debug in the editor, commit with a Conventional Commit message, push and open a pull request, review; changes requested loops back to edit, approved leads to merge and delete the branch.

learning_check.question: A reviewer asks for a change on your open pull request. Where do you go next, and do you open a new pull request?
learning_check.answer: Back to the editor on the same branch. You commit and push again; the open pull request updates, so you do not open a new one.

title: One change from branch to merge

purpose: Compare how merge and rebase join two diverged branches in the commit graph.
explanation: Pro Git 3.2 says a three-way merge combines the two branch tips and their common ancestor into a new snapshot and records a merge commit with more than one parent. Pro Git 3.6 says rebase finds the common ancestor, takes the diff of each commit, resets the branch to the target and applies each change in turn. The final snapshot is the same; the history differs. Arrows point from a commit to its parent.
alt: Graph: C2 and C3 both point to C1. A merge commit M points to both C2 and C3. After rebase, C3 prime points to C2, giving a straight line.

learning_check.question: Both merge and rebase give the same final files. What is different in the history?
learning_check.answer: Merge adds a commit with two parents and keeps both lines of work. Rebase rewrites the branch commits as copies on top of the target, so history is a straight line.

title: Merge versus rebase in the commit graph

purpose: Show how Node.js picks ES module or CommonJS loading for one file, so the learner can predict it.
explanation: Node.js reads the file extension first. A .mjs file is always an ES module and a .cjs file is always CommonJS. For .js it looks at the type field of the nearest package.json. If there is no type field, it runs the file as CommonJS and retries as an ES module when it finds import or export syntax.
alt: Decision diagram: .mjs leads to ES module, .cjs leads to CommonJS, .js depends on the nearest package.json type; module is ESM, commonjs is CommonJS, missing type tries CommonJS and retries as ESM when ES module syntax is found.

learning_check.question: A .js file has no type field in any package.json and contains an import statement. How does Node.js load it?
learning_check.answer: It treats the file as ambiguous, detects the ES module syntax, and loads it as an ES module (syntax detection, with a performance cost). Setting type avoids the guess.

title: Which loader Node.js uses for a file

purpose: Show which commitlint package does which job, so you can plan the same split in a small CLI.
explanation: commitlint splits one check into small packages. The CLI reads the message and exits. The loader builds the config. The lint engine ignores, parses and runs rules. The rules judge one part each. The formatter prints the result. Evidence: cli.ts:298-325, lint.ts:24-178, format.ts:55-93 at commit d2be18a.
alt: Flowchart: a hook or CI job calls the CLI and reader, which load config, then the lint engine; the engine calls the parser and the rules, and the formatter sends the report back to the CLI.

learning_check.question: Which package decides the exit code, and which one decides if a message is valid?
learning_check.answer: The CLI package picks the exit code from the report. The lint engine decides validity from rule results with level 2.

title: commitlint module map

purpose: Follow one commit message from the Git hook to an exit code.
explanation: Git runs the hook, which calls the CLI with the message file. The CLI reads the text, loads the config, lints, formats the report and exits with a number that the hook or CI reads. Evidence: .husky/commit-msg:1, cli.ts:298-405 at commit d2be18a.
alt: Sequence diagram: the commit-msg hook calls the CLI, which reads the message, loads config, asks the lint engine to run each rule, formats the report, and returns exit code 0, 1, 2, 3 or 9 to the hook.

learning_check.question: What does the hook see when the message breaks an error-level rule?
learning_check.answer: A non-zero exit code, 1 by default, and the commit is stopped.

title: commitlint request flow
How text flows through a shell pipeline
purpose: See how each command in a pipeline reads the output of the command before it, and why the order of redirections decides where errors go.
explanation: The pipe connects the standard output of one command to the standard input of the next, and Bash processes redirections in the order you write them.
alt: A seven-line web server log goes through cat access.log | grep 404 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn. grep keeps the five 404 lines, sort puts equal lines together, uniq -c counts each group, and sort -rn puts the largest count first: three errors for /old and two for /logo.png. Then two commands show that Bash processes redirections from left to right, so 2>&1 before or after > out.txt sends the error message to a different place.

learning_check.question: In cat access.log | grep 404 | sort, what does sort read on its standard input?
learning_check.answer: The lines that grep 404 wrote to its standard output, not the file itself.

title: One fork, joined by merge or by rebase
purpose: Show both results of joining the same fork, so the learner can compare the two graphs without the animation.
explanation: C3 on feature and C4 on main both have the parent C2. Merge, run on main, records C5 with the two parents C4 and C3 (Pro Git 3.2). Rebase, run on feature, applies the change of C3 as a new commit C3' with the parent C4, so the history is a straight line (Pro Git 3.6). Arrows point from a commit to its parent.
alt: Commit graph: C3 and C4 point to C2, which points to C1. A merge commit C5 points to both C4 and C3. A rebased commit C3' points only to C4.

learning_check.question: Which result has a commit with two parents, and which one creates a copy of an existing commit?
learning_check.answer: Merge creates C5 with two parents. Rebase creates C3', a new commit that copies the change of C3.

title: Merge and rebase on the same fork
purpose: See how merge and rebase join the same two diverged branches and why the two histories differ.
explanation: A branch is a movable pointer to a commit. Merge adds a commit with two parents and rewrites nothing; rebase copies your commits as new commits on top of the other branch (Pro Git 3.1, 3.2, 3.6).
alt: Commits C1 and C2 sit on main. The branch feature adds C3 and main adds C4, both with the parent C2. On main, git merge feature records a merge commit C5 with the two parents C4 and C3. On feature, git rebase main replays C3 on top of C4 as a new commit C3', so history is a straight line. Both give the same final files, so rebase only commits that exist only in your repository.

learning_check.question: After git rebase main on feature, is C3 still the tip of feature?
learning_check.answer: No. Rebase creates a new commit C3' with the parent C4, and feature now points to C3'. The old C3 is no longer on the branch.

title: The git bisect loop
purpose: Show the git bisect loop as one static diagram for readers without JavaScript.
explanation: You mark one bad commit (often HEAD) and one good older commit. Git checks out a commit in the middle; you test it and mark it good, bad or skip. Each good or bad answer removes about half of the suspect commits, so the loop ends after about log2(n) tests and Git reports the first bad commit (Pro Git, Section 7.10). git bisect reset returns to the commit checked out before git bisect start (git-bisect manual).
alt: Flowchart: git bisect start, mark HEAD bad and c1 good, Git checks out a middle commit, you test it; good or bad leads to a check for one suspect left, which loops back to the middle commit or ends with Git reporting the first bad commit and git bisect reset; skip makes Git pick a nearby commit.

learning_check.question: You mark the middle commit bad. Where can the first bad commit be now?
learning_check.answer: In the tested commit or in an earlier commit after the last good one.

title: Merge or rebase the same two branches
purpose: Predict where each branch and HEAD point after merge or rebase, and say which command rewrites commits.
explanation: Step through an animated walkthrough, change the simulation and answer the checkpoints. Predict where each branch and HEAD point after merge or rebase, and say which command rewrites commits.
alt: A walkthrough and a stepper start from the same fork: C3 on feature and C4 on main, both children of C2. Merge records commit C5 with two parents and rewrites nothing. Rebase replays C3 as a new commit C3' on top of C4, so history is a straight line. A third start shows a merge that stops on a conflict until you edit, add and commit.

learning_check.question: HEAD is on feature and you run git commit. What moves?
learning_check.answer: feature moves to the new commit; HEAD still names feature. HEAD points to the branch you are on, and a new commit moves only that branch pointer forward. Other branches keep pointing at their own commits.

title: git bisect halves the suspect commits at every test
purpose: See how marking one good and one bad commit lets Git find the first bad commit in about four tests out of sixteen.
explanation: Every good or bad answer removes about half of the suspect commits, so 16 commits need about four tests.
alt: A bug is somewhere in 16 commits. You run git bisect start, mark HEAD (c16) bad and c1 good. Git checks out the middle commit; you test it and mark it good or bad. The answers c8 good, c12 bad, c10 good, c11 bad leave one commit: c11 is the first bad commit. git bisect reset returns to the commit you started on. A script can answer for you with git bisect run: exit 0 is good, 1 to 127 except 125 is bad, 125 is skip, any other code aborts.

learning_check.question: c8 is good and c12 is bad. Which commits can still be the first bad commit?
learning_check.answer: c9, c10, c11 and c12: after the last good commit, up to and including the bad one.

title: Find the first bad commit with git bisect
purpose: Mark commits good or bad, predict how many tests bisect needs, and read git bisect run exit codes.
explanation: Step through an animated walkthrough, change the simulation and answer the checkpoints. Mark commits good or bad, predict how many tests bisect needs, and read git bisect run exit codes.
alt: A guided walkthrough of git bisect on 16 commits: mark HEAD bad and c1 good, test the commit Git checks out in the middle, and watch the suspect range halve until one commit is left after four tests. A stepper lets the learner replay the search with the bug in c3, c11 or c16, and with an untestable commit marked skip. The questions cover the step count and the exit codes of git bisect run.

learning_check.question: HEAD (c16) is bad and c1 is good. About how many commits must you test before Git names the first bad commit?
learning_check.answer: About 4. Each answer removes about half of the suspect commits: 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. That is about log2(16) = 4 tests. Pro Git shows the same halving: 6 revisions left, then 3, then 1.

title: Text through the stages of a shell pipeline
purpose: See how each command in a pipeline reads the output of the command before it.
explanation: Each pipe connects one command's standard output to the next command's standard input, so the line count changes from 7 to 5 to 2.
alt: access.log goes into cat, which sends 7 lines to grep 404; grep sends 5 lines to sort; sort sends 5 grouped lines to uniq -c; uniq -c sends 2 counted lines to sort -rn, which prints 3 404 /old and 2 404 /logo.png.

learning_check.question: What does sort read in this pipeline?
learning_check.answer: The five lines that grep 404 wrote, not the file.

title: Build a shell pipeline stage by stage
purpose: Predict the output of each pipeline stage and explain where a redirection sends standard error.
explanation: Step through an animated walkthrough, change the simulation and answer the checkpoints. Predict the output of each pipeline stage and explain where a redirection sends standard error.
alt: A short walkthrough sends a seven-line web server log through cat access.log | grep 404 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn and pauses for predictions. In the stepper, each step shows one stage's standard input next to its standard output. A second trace leaves out sort, and a third shows how Bash processes > out.txt and 2>&1 from left to right, so their order decides where the error message goes.

learning_check.question: grep 404 writes five lines. What does sort write to its standard output in this pipeline?
learning_check.answer: The same five lines, with equal lines next to each other. In a pipeline each command reads the previous command's output through the pipe. sort gets only the five lines grep wrote, and it changes their order, not their number.

title: Bisect run flow
purpose: Show how the script and git bisect run cooperate to find the first bad commit.
explanation: The script find-regression.js starts git bisect with a bad and a good commit. Git checks out commits by binary search and runs check.js. The exit code (0 good, 1 bad, 125 skip) steers the search. At the end the first bad commit is parsed and the repo is reset (git-scm docs, git-bisect).
alt: Flowchart: create demo repo, git bisect start, git bisect run node check.js, check.js returns an exit code back to bisect run, parse first bad commit, git bisect reset.

learning_check.question: What does check.js return for a commit whose price.js has a syntax error?
learning_check.answer: 125, so Git skips that commit instead of calling it bad.

title: GitHub flow for one pull request
purpose: Show the ordered steps of GitHub flow and where review and checks can send a change back.
explanation: GitHub flow (GitHub Docs): create a branch, commit changes, push and open a pull request, address review, merge, then delete the branch. Checks configured on the repository run on the pull request; commitlint runs in CI on the pull request range (.github/workflows/commitlint.yml:46-52 @ d2be18a). New commits update the open pull request.
alt: Flowchart: create branch, commit with a feat message, push and open a pull request, checks run, review; changes asked loops back to commit, approved leads to merge and then delete branch.

learning_check.question: A reviewer asks for a change. Do you open a new pull request?
learning_check.answer: No. You commit and push on the same branch, and the open pull request updates automatically.

title: The safe loop for AI-written code
purpose: Show the gates that AI-written code passes before it is merged: a spec, a failing test, a check that runs, and a human review of every line.
explanation: Claude Code best practices advise a specific prompt, a failing test first, and a pass-or-fail check the agent runs until it passes. A failed check sends the work back to the agent. Then you review the diff against your spec. OWASP LLM05 says to treat model output as untrusted and to review code and suggested packages. Only a diff you can explain line by line goes to merge.
alt: Flowchart from left to right: spec and context, then a failing test, then the agent diff, then run the check. A failed check loops back to the agent diff. A passed check goes to review of every line. An unclear line goes back to the agent, an unsafe one goes back to the spec, and an explained diff goes to merge.

learning_check.question: All tests pass, but one line builds an SQL query by joining strings with user input. Where does the diff go?
learning_check.answer: Back, not to merge. A passing check does not prove safety. OWASP LLM05 says to parameterize queries from model output, so you reject the line or fix the spec and ask again.

title: VS Code settings precedence
purpose: Show which settings scope wins when two scopes set the same setting.
explanation: VS Code docs, Settings precedence: later scopes override earlier ones. The order is Default, User, Remote, Workspace, Workspace Folder. Policy settings from an administrator always win. Language-specific settings sit between Workspace Folder and Policy and are left out here.
alt: Chain of six settings scopes from left to right: Default, User, Remote, Workspace, Workspace Folder, Policy; each scope is overridden by the next, so Policy wins and a workspace value beats a user value.

learning_check.question: Your user settings say tabSize 4 and the project's .vscode/settings.json says 2. Which value applies?
learning_check.answer: 2, because Workspace overrides User.

title: One debug session in VS Code
purpose: Show the loop of a debug session: set a breakpoint, start, pause, inspect, step or continue.
explanation: VS Code docs, Debugging: press F9 to set a breakpoint and F5 to start. Execution pauses at the line; the Variables and Call Stack sections show the state. Step Over (F10) runs one line and pauses again; Continue (F5) runs to the next breakpoint or the end.
alt: Flowchart: set breakpoint with F9, start with F5, pause at the line, inspect variables, then either step over with F10 and pause again, or continue with F5 to the next breakpoint.

learning_check.question: You paused at a breakpoint and want to see the next line change a value. Which key do you press?
learning_check.answer: F10, Step Over, which runs the current line and pauses again.

title: Commit-msg hook lint flow
purpose: Show how a commit-msg hook turns a commit message into an exit code.
explanation: Git runs the commit-msg hook with the message file. cli.js reads it, hook.js removes comment lines, lint.js parses the message and runs the rules, and exitCodeFor returns 0 or 1. Git blocks the commit on a non-zero code (Conventional Commits 1.0.0; git-scm githooks).
alt: Flowchart: commit-msg hook calls cli.js runCli, which calls stripComments, then lint with parse and rules, then exitCodeFor, whose exit code returns to the hook.

learning_check.question: Which exit code makes Git stop the commit, and which function chooses it?
learning_check.answer: Any non-zero code; exitCodeFor returns 1 when the message has an error.

purpose: Show the four layers of devkit and which layer depends on which.
explanation: The devkit code has a domain core, an application layer with three use cases, an infrastructure layer for the real machine and Git, and an interface layer for the CLI. main.js wires them. Dependencies point inward, so the commit and version logic never imports Git or the file system.
alt: Flowchart: main.js wires the interface and infrastructure layers; interface depends on application; infrastructure and application both depend on the domain core, so the domain imports nothing.

learning_check.question: Which layer may import node:child_process, and why not the domain?
learning_check.answer: Only infrastructure (SystemEnvironment, GitCommitSource) may. The domain stays pure, so tests run with fakes and without Git.

title: Layers of the devkit CLI

purpose: Show what happens from the commit-msg hook to the exit code.
explanation: Git runs devkit with the message file. The Cli asks GitCommitSource for the message, LintCommitsUseCase parses it and asks CommitRules to check it, and the Report decides the exit code. Exit 0 lets the commit continue. Exit 1 stops it and prints each problem.
alt: Sequence diagram: the Git hook calls Cli, which reads the message through GitCommitSource, passes it to LintCommitsUseCase and CommitRules, then returns a Report that becomes exit code 0 or 1 for Git.

learning_check.question: What stops the commit when a message is invalid?
learning_check.answer: The exit code 1 that Cli returns after Report.exitCode() sees an error-level result.

title: Request flow of devkit lint --edit

purpose: Show the three places that run the same devkit process and what it reads.
explanation: devkit is one short Node.js process. A developer starts it in a terminal, a commit-msg hook starts it before each commit, and a CI job starts it on a pull request range. It calls the git program and reads DEVKIT_ environment variables as its only configuration.
alt: Flowchart: a developer terminal, the commit-msg hook and a CI job all start node src/main.js, which calls the git program and reads DEVKIT environment variables.

learning_check.question: Why does the CI job use fetch-depth 0?
learning_check.answer: A shallow clone hides commits, so GitCommitSource.range stops with an error. Full history lets CI lint every commit of the pull request.

title: Where devkit runs
